topic.title: PJM's 'Bring Your Own Power' Mandate: Has US Grid Interconnection Policy Overtaken Equipment Supply as AI Data Centers' Binding Constraint?
topic.trigger: PJM Interconnection -- the largest US grid operator, covering roughly 65 million people -- filed a proposed 'Interim Resource Adequacy Service' (IRAS) and Large Load Registry with FERC (Docket ER26-3380) on August 13, 2026, following a Board of Managers decisional letter on July 27, 2026. The filing would make any new data center or other 'Large Load' of 50MW or more that does not secure its own qualifying generation, storage, or contracted capacity (Bring Your Own New Capacity, or 'BYONC') first in line for involuntary curtailment ahead of ordinary residential and commercial demand-response measures, starting June 1, 2027. This follows FERC's unprecedented June 18, 2026 show-cause orders (Docket RM26-4) to all six US grid operators to justify or reform their large-load interconnection rules within 60 days, and lands the same week PJM's own capacity auction data show data centers driving a record $333.44/MW-day clearing price and PJM's first-ever reliability shortfall. This is a distinct, non-duplicative angle on the AI buildout's power constraint this pipeline has not yet examined: a policy-driven capacity-allocation mechanism, not a physical-equipment shortage like the grid-transformer bottleneck covered on 2026-08-23.

questions.primary: Does PJM's FERC-filed Interim Resource Adequacy Service / 'Bring Your Own New Capacity' (BYONC) curtailment framework mark a shift from physical-equipment scarcity to a policy-created capacity-allocation constraint that will bind AI data center buildout in the largest US grid -- and is that constraint durable, or a contestable proposal likely to be watered down before it ever takes effect?
sub: What exactly does PJM's August 13, 2026 FERC filing (Interim Resource Adequacy Service, IRAS) require of new 'Large Loads' of 50MW+ after June 1, 2027, and what qualifies as BYONC?

How does this policy-layer constraint relate to -- and interact with -- the physical grid-equipment shortage (transformers, electrical steel) this pipeline covered on 2026-08-23, and the gas-turbine backlog behind on-site self-generation?

What is driving PJM specifically: how large is the capacity-auction price run-up and reliability shortfall, and how much of requested data-center load is real versus 'phantom' per independent forecasters?
Is this a PJM-only phenomenon, or is FERC's broader June 2026 show-cause order producing similar rules at other grid operators (MISO, ERCOT, SPP, ISO-NE, NYISO, CAISO)?
What would falsify the thesis that this is a durable structural constraint, given PJM's own history of softening an earlier mandatory bring-your-own-generation proposal after stakeholder pushback?

thesis: PJM's FERC filing for an Interim Resource Adequacy Service that would curtail new 50MW+ 'Large Loads' ahead of ordinary demand-response unless they secure Bring-Your-Own-New-Capacity is not itself the bottleneck -- it is a rationing mechanism that reveals a genuine, pre-existing structural bottleneck in firm, dispatchable generation capacity within the largest US grid, evidenced by PJM's capacity-auction clearing price rising more than tenfold in three years (to a record $333.44/MW-day) and its first-ever failure to clear enough capacity to meet its own reliability requirement (a roughly 6,600MW shortfall). Because gas-turbine lead times (three-plus years, backlogs into 2029-2031 at GE Vernova, Siemens Energy and Mitsubishi Power) are now the binding constraint on the BYONC self-generation path meant to satisfy PJM's rule, the policy does not create new supply -- it allocates scarcity, shifting risk onto AI data-center developers and, indirectly, onto Nvidia's downstream GPU-cluster deployment timelines. The framework's durability is genuinely contested: it does not bind until June 1, 2027, applies only to new loads, and PJM itself abandoned a mandatory bring-your-own-generation proposal for a voluntary one after 2025 stakeholder pushback, so FERC approval, legal challenge, or further softening before mid-2027 are all live risks.

facts.statement: On June 18, 2026, FERC issued six separate Section 206 show-cause orders (Docket RM26-4) to all US FERC-jurisdictional grid operators (PJM, MISO, SPP, CAISO, ISO-NE, NYISO), giving each 60 days (to August 17, 2026) to justify why existing tariffs adequately address large-load (20MW+) interconnection or propose reforms, plus a 30-day reliability report on securing generation capacity for large loads. The orders cover roughly 200 million people across 30+ states -- about two-thirds of FERC-jurisdictional load.

PJM's Board of Managers issued a decisional letter on July 27, 2026 directing PJM staff to file a Reliability Backstop Procurement framework and an 'Interim Resource Adequacy Service' (IRAS) with FERC. PJM filed the core framework under Docket ER26-3380 beginning July 31, 2026, followed by the specific IRAS proposal and a new Large Load Registry on August 13, 2026.

PJM's IRAS proposal defines a 'Large Load' as end-use demand with a cumulative peak of at least 50MW at a single electrical site (within a one-mile radius), and a 'New Large Load' as one entering service after June 1, 2027. Under the proposal, any portion of a New Large Load's demand not backed by qualifying new capacity -- on-site generation, a long-term power contract, or purchased PJM-market capacity, collectively 'Bring Your Own New Capacity' (BYONC) -- would be curtailed before Pre-Emergency Load Management is deployed on ordinary customers during a capacity shortage.

PJM requested a FERC-approved effective date of October 12, 2026 for the tariff revisions, to give it time to build the administrative framework before the IRAS/BYONC curtailment mechanism itself takes effect for New Large Loads on June 1, 2027.

PJM's capacity-auction clearing price rose from $28.92/MW-day (2024/2025 delivery year) to $269.92/MW-day (2025/2026) to $329.17/MW-day (2026/2027) to a record $333.44/MW-day (2027/2028), with PJM's own market monitor attributing roughly 40% ($6.5 billion of a total $16.4 billion) of the most recent auction's cleared cost to data-center load.

PJM's 2027/2028 delivery-year capacity auction cleared roughly 6,623MW less than PJM's own Reliability Requirement -- reported as the first time in PJM's history that an auction failed to fully meet its reliability target.

As of its Q2 2026 earnings call (late July 2026), GE Vernova reported a 116GW gas-power-equipment backlog (53GW firm orders, 63GW paid slot reservations), up from 100GW three months earlier and 83GW at end-2025, and guided to at least 125GW under contract by December 2026; ordering a heavy-duty gas turbine from GE Vernova today results in delivery not before 2031. Siemens Energy reported a 69GW firm gas-turbine backlog as of its fiscal Q3 (ended June 30, 2026); Mitsubishi Heavy Industries reported a 35GW large-frame turbine backlog (up from 23GW a year earlier), with orders booked in the quarter scheduled for 2028-2030 delivery.

A Bloomberg analysis published August 12, 2026, citing Wood Mackenzie, estimated that of 1,066GW of electricity requested for US data-center projects, grid operators and utilities are likely to actually commit to only about 28% (roughly 299GW), with the remaining ~768GW characterized as 'phantom load' from speculative or duplicate project pitches that will not materialize.

Texas's ERCOT market took a parallel but distinct approach: the Public Utility Commission of Texas approved rules on June 18, 2026 for an initial 'Batch Zero' large-load interconnection process requiring transmission-voltage customers connecting after December 31, 2025 to accept curtailment during firm load-shed events (unless designated critical); ERCOT received 198GW of large-load interconnection applications in Q1 2026 alone, with 86GW under active review.

On August 26, 2026, Anthropic agreed to pay Nscale $45 billion over six years for 460MW of AI compute capacity (running Nvidia's Vera Rubin chips) at Nscale's 'Monarch' data-center campus in Mason County, West Virginia -- reported as the latest in a series of Anthropic compute deals that secure dedicated capacity ahead of grid-connection risk, following an earlier $10 billion deal with Volta for capacity in Norway.

PJM's current large-load framework follows an earlier, more contested stakeholder process in which PJM had proposed a mandatory bring-your-own-generation (BYOG) requirement; after 'clear, overall stakeholder concern,' PJM shifted to a voluntary framework before the current, more binding IRAS/BYONC proposal was filed in mid-2026. Consumer advocates (e.g., Citizens Utility Board) and some state officials have criticized the current plan for leaving key implementation questions to individual states.

inferences.statement: Because PJM's capacity-auction clearing price rose more than tenfold in three years and the grid failed for the first time to clear its full reliability requirement, the underlying constraint predates and is independent of PJM's IRAS filing -- the filing is a rationing/allocation mechanism responding to an already-binding scarcity of firm dispatchable capacity, not the cause of that scarcity.

Because BYONC compliance can be satisfied via a long-term power contract or purchased PJM-market capacity rather than only new on-site generation, and because GE Vernova, Siemens Energy and Mitsubishi Power gas-turbine lead times run three to five years, most New Large Loads reaching PJM's June 1, 2027 binding date will likely satisfy BYONC through contracts/purchased capacity rather than newly built on-site turbines -- meaning the rule's near-term effect is more a reallocation of existing capacity toward well-capitalized developers than a direct trigger for new physical generation build.

Because Wood Mackenzie estimates roughly 72% of requested US data-center power is 'phantom load,' PJM's own large-load interconnection queue and reliability-shortfall projections likely embed some of that inflation, meaning the true scale of the binding constraint may be smaller than headline gigawatt figures suggest, even though the auction price and shortfall data indicate a real, not purely speculative, shortfall exists today.

Because PJM previously retreated from a mandatory bring-your-own-generation requirement to a voluntary one after stakeholder pushback, and because the current IRAS proposal still requires FERC approval by the requested October 12, 2026 effective date with the binding curtailment mechanism itself not applying until June 1, 2027, there is a meaningful multi-quarter window in which the rule's final, binding form could still be softened, delayed, or legally challenged before it constrains any actual data-center project.

unknowns: Whether FERC will approve PJM's ER26-3380/IRAS filing as proposed, modify it, or reject it was not resolved by any source gathered in this research pass -- FERC's ruling had not been reported as of August 28, 2026.

The precise number or aggregate MW of specific, named AI data-center projects that would be immediately subject to New-Large-Load curtailment risk under the June 1, 2027 effective date (as opposed to projects grandfathered by connecting earlier) was not found in any source gathered.

Whether MISO, SPP, ISO-NE, NYISO and CAISO will adopt comparable curtailment-priority/BYONC-style frameworks in response to FERC's RM26-4 show-cause order, or materially weaker rules, remained unresolved in the sources gathered as of this research pass.

The specific historical timeline and stakeholder-comment details of PJM's earlier 2025 mandatory-to-voluntary BYOG reversal (exact dates, vote counts, which stakeholders drove the change) were not independently confirmed beyond a single secondary source's summary.

Every primary-source fetch attempted in this research pass (ferc.gov, pjm.com filing PDFs and board disclosures, sec.gov, and several law-firm and trade-press domains) was blocked by the research environment's egress proxy; all facts rely on convergent web-search-result snippets rather than directly retrieved primary documents.

industry_chain.name: Firm/dispatchable generation capacity (gas turbines, gas supply, nuclear uprates)
Grid interconnection, tariff design & capacity-market administration

bottlenecks.expansion_time: 3-5 years for new gas-turbine capacity (GE Vernova lead times run to 2031; Mitsubishi orders booked for 2028-2030 delivery)
bottlenecks.rationale: Meets the strict three-part test: demand growth is extreme (capacity-auction clearing price rose more than tenfold in three years to a record $333.44/MW-day, and the grid failed for the first time to clear its full reliability requirement); supply elasticity is low because new firm capacity requires multi-year turbine lead times and permitting; substitutability is hard because renewables and short-duration storage cannot fully replace firm, dispatchable capacity for grid-reliability purposes at the scale and timeline required.

bottlenecks.node: Grid interconnection & tariff/curtailment-rule administration (PJM IRAS and FERC's broader RM26-4 process)
bottlenecks.expansion_time: months for a FERC ruling; PJM's own requested effective date is October 12, 2026 with the binding mechanism applying from June 1, 2027
bottlenecks.rationale: Demand for large-load interconnection is high (198GW of ERCOT requests in Q1 2026 alone; PJM building a new Large Load Registry), but the process itself has medium elasticity -- FERC can approve, modify or reject rules on a multi-month timeline -- and medium substitutability, since developers can route new projects to other RTOs/ISOs or off-grid configurations, so it does not meet the strict Hard-substitutability bar for a Structural Bottleneck.

bottlenecks.expansion_time: 3-5 years for new gas turbines from the three dominant OEMs (GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, Mitsubishi Power)
bottlenecks.rationale: BYONC-driven demand for new turbines is extreme and turbine supply elasticity is low, but substitutability is only medium because PJM's BYONC definition also accepts long-term power-purchase contracts and purchased PJM-market capacity, giving developers routes to compliance that do not require building new on-site generation -- so this node falls short of the strict Hard-substitutability test.

companies.name: PJM Interconnection
companies.business_model: Nonprofit regional transmission organization operating the wholesale electricity market and transmission grid for roughly 65 million people across 13 US states and Washington, D.C.; not a publicly traded company.
companies.revenue_model: Funded by market administration fees and tariff charges on generators, load-serving entities and transmission owners, not by equity/debt capital markets in the way a public company is.
growth_drivers: Rapid AI/data-center load growth driving record capacity-auction prices
FERC's June 2026 show-cause order compelling tariff reform
New Large Load Registry and IRAS administrative build-out
companies.moat: Sole grid operator and capacity-market administrator for its multi-state footprint; regulatory authority derives from its FERC-approved tariff rather than a competitive market position.
companies.switching_costs: High for generators, load-serving entities and large loads physically connected to PJM's footprint; a developer can choose a different RTO or off-grid site only for a new project, not an existing one.
companies.management_strategy: Filed the Interim Resource Adequacy Service and Large Load Registry with FERC to prioritize reliability for existing customers over new, uncommitted large loads while pushing some implementation questions to individual states.
companies.execution_risk: PJM previously retreated from a mandatory bring-your-own-generation proposal to a voluntary one after stakeholder pushback in 2025, indicating a track record of the rule's binding elements being negotiated down before final implementation.

competitors.note: Can partially qualify as BYONC capacity for shorter-duration reliability needs without the 3-5 year lead times of new gas turbines, though duration and scale limits constrain full substitution for firm generation.

bear_case.argument: PJM already retreated once from a mandatory bring-your-own-generation requirement to a voluntary framework after 2025 stakeholder pushback, and FERC could similarly modify, delay or reject the current IRAS/BYONC proposal before its requested October 12, 2026 effective date.

Wood Mackenzie estimates roughly 72% of the 1,066GW of US data-center power currently requested is 'phantom load' that will never materialize, suggesting the scale of demand pressure driving PJM's rule may be significantly overstated relative to what actually gets built.

The IRAS curtailment mechanism does not bind until June 1, 2027 and applies only to New Large Loads, giving developers roughly ten months to secure grandfathered interconnection, lock in BYONC-qualifying contracts, or lobby for further changes before any project faces actual curtailment risk.

BYONC can be satisfied through long-term power contracts or purchased PJM-market capacity, not only new on-site generation, so the three-to-five-year gas-turbine lead times at GE Vernova, Siemens Energy and Mitsubishi Power do not necessarily gate compliance for most developers.

Developers can route new large loads to other RTOs/ISOs with different rules (e.g., ERCOT's curtailment-acceptance-based process) or to off-grid, behind-the-meter configurations entirely, potentially arbitraging away PJM-specific policy risk rather than being bound by it.

kill_conditions.condition: FERC rejects or materially waters down PJM's IRAS/BYONC proposal
kill_conditions.threshold: FERC denies the mandatory curtailment-priority framework, requires it be made voluntary, or orders substantial revisions removing the BYONC-linked curtailment priority

kill_conditions.metric: PJM Base Residual Auction cleared capacity vs. Reliability Requirement
kill_conditions.threshold: A subsequent PJM capacity auction fully clears its Reliability Requirement with no shortfall

kill_conditions.metric: Reported order-to-delivery lead time at GE Vernova, Siemens Energy and Mitsubishi Power
kill_conditions.threshold: Quoted lead times fall below 2 years at two or more of the three major OEMs

kill_conditions.condition: New large loads bypass PJM en masse for other RTOs or off-grid siting
kill_conditions.metric: Reported large-load interconnection queue volumes by RTO/ISO
kill_conditions.threshold: PJM's share of new US large-load interconnection requests falls materially quarter over quarter relative to ERCOT/MISO/off-grid alternatives

kill_conditions.condition: Independent analysis confirms realized data-center load growth in PJM falls well below current planning assumptions
kill_conditions.metric: Independent load-forecast reconciliation studies (e.g., Wood Mackenzie, PJM's own load forecast revisions)
kill_conditions.threshold: Realized/contracted large-load growth in PJM comes in well below current capacity-auction-driving forecasts for two or more consecutive planning cycles

sources.claim: ERCOT's parallel large-load interconnection and curtailment-acceptance framework
sources.source_title: Utility Dive: "Texas, facing 438 GW queue, approves initial large-load interconnection process"
sources.quote_or_extract: LIMITATION: direct fetch of utilitydive.com was blocked by the research environment's egress proxy. Search-result snippet: the Public Utility Commission of Texas approved rules on June 18, 2026 for ERCOT's initial 'Batch Zero' large-load interconnection process; transmission-voltage customers interconnecting after December 31, 2025 must accept curtailment during firm load-shed events unless designated critical; ERCOT received 198GW of large-load interconnection applications in Q1 2026 alone, with 86GW under active review, against a total queue described elsewhere as 438GW.
